content.title: About
content.content: A calzone is a folded pizza shaped like a half‑moon, filled with cheese and various toppings. This version contains only cheese and no meat, making it vegetarian. The dough is made from wheat flour, water, yeast, and olive oil, and after being stuffed it is baked until golden and crisp.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Calzones originate from Naples, where they are called “calzone” (Italian for “belt”).
Traditionally they were made from leftover pizza dough and toppings.
Unlike open‑face pizza, a calzone is baked closed, which traps moisture and flavor inside.
There are countless filling variations, from classic mozzarella and tomato to vegetables, mushrooms, and seafood.
In the United States calzones are often served with a dipping sauce, whereas in Italy they are usually eaten plain.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cheese filling provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cheese supplies high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: If a cheese with live cultures is used, it can support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Unlike sweet pastries, a calzone contains virtually no added sugar, making it better for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the dough and fats from the cheese provides lasting satiety and energy.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Cheese and dough make the dish calorie‑dense and high in fat; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese contains lactose, which can cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat dough contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese is often salty; individuals with high blood pressure should choose low‑salt varieties.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the calzone hot, sliced in half. It can be eaten with hands like a pizza or with a knife and fork. It pairs well with marinara sauce, a fresh side salad, or a light vegetable accompaniment.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in an oven or air‑fryer to restore a crisp crust. It can be frozen for up to 1 month, wrapped tightly in plastic film and foil.

coffee-iced-latte-decaffeinated-nonfat-f.title: Coffee, Iced Latte, Decaffeinated, Nonfat, Flavored

content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated iced latte is a cold beverage made from espresso diluted with nonfat milk and flavored with natural extracts (e.g., vanilla, caramel). The caffeine is removed through a specialized process while preserving the coffee’s flavor profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaf coffee retains most of the antioxidants found in regular coffee.
Nonfat milk reduces calories but still provides protein and calcium.
Flavored versions often use natural extracts rather than artificial flavors.
Cold serving enhances perceived sweetness, so less sugar is needed.
Decaffeination can be done by water, CO₂, or solvent methods.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support vascular health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Nonfat milk and the absence of added sugar make the drink suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Even nonfat milk supplies calcium essential for bone health.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: A cold beverage encourages fluid intake, especially in warm weather.

items.title: Less stomach irritation
items.content: Without caffeine, the drink is less likely to cause heartburn or excess acidity.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or casein allergy should choose a dairy‑free alternative.

items.title: Artificial flavor content
items.content: Some flavored versions may contain synthetic additives that can trigger sensitivities.

items.title: Residual decaffeination agents
items.content: Solvent‑based decaffeination can leave trace amounts of chemicals if not properly removed.

items.title: Reduced flavor depth
items.content: Lack of caffeine sometimes results in a less robust taste, which may disappoint strong‑coffee fans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the decaf iced latte chilled over ice in a glass. Add a splash of sweetener, fresh fruit, or a sprinkle of cinnamon if desired. It can also be used as a base for smoothies, replacing part of the fruit with milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared drink refrigerated and consume within 24 hours. Do not freeze, as the milk texture may separate. Store milk and flavor extracts according to their package instructions.

content.title: About
content.content: Croaker (*Sciaenidae*) is a marine fish found in coastal waters of the Pacific and Atlantic oceans. It has an elongated body covered with fine scales and produces a characteristic “drumming” sound by contracting muscles around its swim bladder.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Croaker belongs to the Sciaenidae family, which also includes drum and sea bass species.
The sound it produces is used in courtship rituals and territorial displays.
The fish can change its coloration depending on environment and stress level.
Croaker is widely used in Asian cuisines, especially in Japan and China.
In some regions it is considered an indicator of water quality because of its sensitivity to pollution.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Croaker provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: It contains EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in B12, B6 and niacin, which aid normal metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides selenium, iodine and phosphorus, important for thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Low mercury levels
items.content: Compared with larger predatory fish, croaker typically has lower mercury, making it safer for regular consumption.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including croaker.

items.title: Water contamination
items.content: Fish caught in polluted areas can contain heavy metals and microplastics.

items.title: Parasites
items.content: As with any raw fish, there is a risk of parasites; proper cooking eliminates this hazard.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Croaker can be pan‑fried, baked, steamed, or used in soups and stews. Fillets without bones are convenient for quick meals, while whole fish is often marinated with soy sauce and ginger before grilling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh croaker should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C and used within 2 days. For longer storage, freeze the fish in an airtight bag at –18 °C; thaw in the refrigerator before cooking.

fruit-and-vegetable-smoothie-added-prote.title: Fruit and vegetable smoothie, added protein

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit and vegetable smoothie with added protein is a ready‑to‑drink blend of fresh fruits, vegetables and plant or whey protein. It is designed to quickly replenish energy and support muscle growth after workouts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The smoothie combines vitamins and minerals from fruits and vegetables with a complete source of protein.
The protein is often enriched with branched‑chain amino acids (BCAA) that aid muscle recovery.
Typical ingredients include spinach, kiwi, banana and pea protein.
Convenient for on‑the‑go consumption: it can be taken in a bottle and drunk anytime.
Sugar content is controlled by using low‑sugar fruits and natural sweeteners.

items.title: Supports muscle growth
items.content: Protein provides essential amino acids needed for muscle protein synthesis, especially after exercise.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: Fruits and vegetables supply vitamin C, vitamin A, folate and antioxidants that protect cells.

items.title: Improves digestion
items.content: Fiber from the fruit and vegetable blend supports healthy gut function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Quick energy replenishment
items.content: The combination of fruit carbohydrates and protein delivers fast and sustained energy.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamins and minerals such as vitamin C, zinc and iron help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to dairy or plant‑based protein.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Formulations with many sweet fruits can raise blood sugar levels; low‑glycemic options are recommended.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of fiber may cause bloating or discomfort in sensitive people.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Protein smoothies can be calorie‑dense; portion size should fit within daily energy needs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the smoothie immediately after preparation or store it in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. It is convenient to pour into a sports bottle and consume before or right after a workout.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared smoothie in an airtight bottle in the fridge at 0–4 °C. Before drinking, check for off‑flavors or sour smell; discard if any signs of spoilage appear.

content.title: About
content.content: A ham sandwich on wheat is a classic sandwich made with slices of cooked ham, fresh vegetables (usually tomato, cucumber and lettuce) and a spread, placed between two slices of whole‑grain wheat bread. It is popular as a quick lunch or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat bread provides slow‑release energy thanks to complex carbohydrates.
Ham prepared without nitrites contains fewer potentially harmful compounds.
Ham sandwiches are a staple in school cafeterias and sports events.
Adding lettuce boosts vitamin K and fiber content.
Ham is a good source of protein that helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Ham supplies high‑quality animal protein needed for tissue repair and immune function.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Ham provides thiamine, niacin and vitamin B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from ham aids oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Dietary fiber from whole‑grain wheat bread
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat bread adds fiber that benefits digestion.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Unlike many processed snacks, a ham sandwich typically contains no added sugars.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham is often salty, which can be an issue for people with high blood pressure.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some hams are cured with nitrites, which may be harmful in large amounts.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, making the sandwich unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich can be calorie‑rich, especially when high‑fat spreads are added.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich cold or lightly toasted. Add mustard, mayo, or a yogurt‑based spread to taste. For variety, include avocado, cheese, or hummus.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Store bread and ham separately when possible to prevent sogginess.

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed olives are olives, usually green or black, filled with various fillings such as cheese, nuts, spices, or meat pastes. They combine the characteristic salty flavor of olives with the aroma of the stuffing and are often served as an appetizer or used as an ingredient in dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffed olives are popular in Mediterranean cuisine, especially in Italy, Spain and Greece.
Traditional fillings include feta cheese, anchovies, almonds, garlic and aromatic herbs.
Olives contain polyphenols that give them antioxidant properties.
In ancient Roman cuisine olives were often stuffed with spices and honey.
Stuffed olives are frequently used in cocktails, for example in a martini.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Olives provide monounsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols and vitamin E in olives help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in olives promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Contains iron and copper
items.content: These minerals are involved in hemoglobin formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate sodium content
items.content: The salt used in brining can help maintain electrolyte balance, but should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Stuffed olives are often very salty, which can be an issue for people with hypertension.

items.title: Olive allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to olives or to the fillings.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some commercial varieties contain preservatives that may cause sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Olives are calorie‑dense due to their fat content, so they should be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stuffed olives are served as a snack, added to salads, pastas, pizza, tapas and cocktails. They can also be incorporated into hot dishes such as casseroles or risotto to add flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep olives in the original jar or a sealed glass container in the refrigerator. Once opened, consume within 1‑2 weeks. Discard if mold, off‑smell, or taste changes appear.

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potato ready‑to‑heat with gravy is a pre‑cooked mash made from selected potatoes, blended with a smooth gravy. It is sealed in an airtight package, retains its aroma and flavor, and can be heated in just a few minutes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mash is made from whole potatoes without artificial colourings.
The gravy typically contains natural broth, cream and spices, giving the dish a richer taste.
Flash‑freezing technology preserves up to 95 % of the vitamins and minerals found in fresh potatoes.
The product is widely used in cafeterias, hotels and homes as a quick side dish.
Ready‑to‑heat mashed potatoes appeared in Russia in the 1990s and have become a staple for busy consumers.

items.title: Rich source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are high in potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Despite heat processing, the mash retains some vitamin C, important for the immune system.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates for energy
items.content: Complex carbs provide a steady release of energy.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When paired with a low‑fat gravy, the dish can fit into a low‑fat diet.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: A modest amount of fiber aids digestion.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready‑made mash often contains added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Allergens in gravy
items.content: The gravy may contain dairy or gluten; always check the label if you have sensitivities.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some versions include preservatives that could trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Overheating
items.content: Overheating can make the mash dry and diminish its flavor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the mash in the microwave or on the stovetop, stirring until smooth. Serve as a side with meat, fish or vegetable dishes. For extra flavor, add butter, cheese or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package in the freezer for up to 6 months. Once opened, store in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑4 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is a plant native to western South America whose juicy fruits are eaten around the world. Tomatoes are usually red but can also be yellow, orange, green, pink, or purple. They have a balanced sweet and tangy flavor and are eaten raw, cooked, or processed into sauces, pastes, juices, and ketchup.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Botanically, a tomato is a fruit, classified as a type of berry, though it is used as a vegetable in cooking.
Tomatoes were introduced to Europe in the 16th century after being brought from the Americas.
Thousands of tomato varieties exist, differing in size, color, and flavor.
The red color comes mainly from lycopene, a pigment that becomes easier to absorb when tomatoes are cooked.
Tomatoes are one of the most widely grown and consumed vegetable crops in the world.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is an antioxidant found in tomatoes that helps protect cells against oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes contain vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains potassium and folate
items.content: These nutrients support normal blood pressure and cell function.

items.title: Provides vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports normal blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Tomatoes are low in calories and high in water, making them refreshing and filling.

items.title: Acid reflux
items.content: Tomatoes are acidic and may trigger heartburn or reflux in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people may experience itching or tingling in the mouth or other allergic reactions.

items.title: Salt and sugar in processed products
items.content: Sauces, canned tomatoes, and ketchup may contain added salt or sugar.

items.title: Potassium considerations
items.content: People on a potassium-restricted diet or taking certain medications should consult a healthcare professional about their intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tomatoes can be eaten fresh in salads and sandwiches, sliced with salt and herbs, or cooked into soups, sauces, stews, and baked dishes. They can also be dried, roasted, or made into juice and paste. Cooking tomatoes with a little olive oil may improve lycopene absorption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unripe tomatoes at room temperature, away from direct sunlight, until they ripen. Ripe tomatoes can be kept at room temperature for a few days or refrigerated for slightly longer, though cold can affect flavor and texture. Cut tomatoes should be refrigerated in an airtight container. Tomatoes can also be cooked and frozen.

turkey-and-ham-sandwich-on-white-with-ch.title: Turkey and Ham Sandwich on White Bread with Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: The sandwich consists of slices of turkey and ham placed between two pieces of white bread, with melted cheese added. It is a quick and nutritious option for lunch or a snack, providing protein, carbohydrates, and a modest amount of fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is considered a leaner meat compared with beef, making it popular in diet-friendly sandwiches.
Ham, derived from pork, gives the sandwich its characteristic savory flavor.
White bread offers a soft texture but contains less fiber than whole‑grain varieties.
Turkey‑and‑ham sandwiches are common in school cafeterias and at sporting events because they are easy to handle.
Adding cheese boosts calcium content and adds a creamy taste.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Turkey and ham provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry and pork contain B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, important for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: White bread supplies quickly digestible carbs that give an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, this sandwich contains virtually no added sugars.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham and cheese are often salty, which can be a concern for people with high blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: The saturated fat in ham and cheese may raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: White bread contains gluten, making the sandwich unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich cold or lightly toasted. Add lettuce, tomato, or mustard for extra flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, keep the bread and fillings separate.
